tldr: DiffuserLite introduces a progressive refinement planning (PRP) process that generates trajectories coarsely then refines them step-by-step, reducing redundant information modeling and achieving real-time diffusion planning at 122.2Hz (112.7x faster than Diffuser and DD) while maintaining SOTA performance on D4RL benchmarks.
contributions: Introduction of plan refinement process (PRP) for coarse-to-fine-grained trajectory generation, reducing modeling of redundant information.
Introduction of DiffuserLite, a lightweight diffusion planning framework that significantly increases decision-making frequency via PRP.
Demonstration that DiffuserLite is a simple and flexible plugin easily combined with other diffusion planning algorithms.
Achievement of 122.2Hz average decision-making frequency (112.7x faster than predominant frameworks) and SOTA performance across multiple D4RL benchmarks.
methods: The authors propose progressive refinement planning (PRP), which performs rough planning by considering only states at distant intervals, then iteratively refines the first interval by generative interpolation until reaching step-level resolution across L levels. They use a DiT backbone instead of UNet due to reduced sequence lengths (typically ~5), conditional sampling via classifier-free guidance (CFG) for speed, and an inverse dynamic model for action extraction. Optionally, rectified flow is integrated to enable one-step sampling. Three backbone variations were implemented: standard diffusion (D), rectified flow (R1), and rectified flow with reflow (R2), trained on publicly available offline RL datasets.
results: DiffuserLite achieves an average decision-making frequency of 122.2Hz (R2 backbone), compared to 1.3Hz for Diffuser and 0.4Hz for DD — a 112.7x speedup. Runtime cost was 0.51% of Diffuser/DD on average. On FrankaKitchen sub-tasks, success rates improved by [41.5%, 56.2%, 55.3%, 8.7%] over Diffuser while being 200-300x faster. On D4RL, DiffuserLite achieved SOTA performance across all benchmarks, with notable gains in MuJoCo sub-optimal datasets and long-horizon Antmaze tasks.
limitations: Sparse reward tasks pose challenges where cumulative reward alone can confuse diffusion models, though addressed with discounted rewards and value function augmentation.
HDMI results required reproduction since original code was not open-sourced, potentially affecting comparison accuracy.
The approach assumes redundancy in distant trajectory segments, which may not hold universally across all task domains.
